title: Stack Applications: Parentheses & Expressions
summary: The first real patterns a stack unlocks: matching nested structures and evaluating expressions — validating brackets, converting infix to postfix, and building a basic calculator.

slides.markdown:
A stack's LIFO discipline is a perfect match for anything **nested** — the last thing opened must be the first thing closed, whether that's a bracket, a function call, or an operator precedence rule.

This topic covers the two families of problems that pattern unlocks first: validating and matching nested structures (balanced parentheses, next-greater-element previews of the monotonic-stack topic), and evaluating expressions written with operators and parentheses (postfix evaluation, infix-to-postfix conversion, a basic calculator).

Both families reduce to the same instinct: when you see something that must be resolved in reverse-nesting order, reach for a stack before reaching for anything else.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a stack fits nested structures
slides.markdown:
Nesting has a defining property: the most recently opened structure must be the first one closed. `([{}])` is valid because each closer matches the innermost still-open opener; `([)]` is invalid because `)` tries to close `[`, which isn't the innermost.

A stack tracks "still open, waiting to be closed" exactly in the order that matters: push on open, and a close must match whatever is currently on top. If it doesn't, the nesting is broken. This is the same reason a call stack unwinds inner function calls before outer ones, and the same reason HTML/XML tag validation is a stack problem — any "must close in reverse order of opening" structure is this pattern.

slides.sectionTitle: Checking bracket counts instead of order and type
The next greater element, brute force
slides.subTitle: Why it screams for a smarter stack-based approach
slides.markdown:
"For every element, find the next element to its right that's greater" has an obvious O(n²) solution: for each index, scan rightward until you find a bigger value. It works, but it repeats work — the same rightward scan gets re-run from scratch for every starting index, even though many of those scans are answering questions that later, smarter bookkeeping could answer in one pass.

The tell that a smarter approach exists: once you know element X's next-greater is Y, and you later meet an even bigger element Z, Z is *also* the answer for X and possibly several elements before X — a fact the brute force never reuses. Keeping a stack of "elements still waiting for their next-greater" turns this insight into a single O(n) pass, covered in full in the `monotonic-stack` topic that follows this one.

slides.subTitle: With a single stack
slides.markdown:
Postfix (Reverse Polish) notation writes operators **after** their operands: `3 4 +` means 3 + 4, and `3 4 + 2 *` means (3 + 4) * 2. No parentheses are needed because the order of operations is already encoded by position — every operator applies to whatever two values were most recently produced.

Evaluation is one left-to-right pass with a single stack: push numbers as you see them; when you see an operator, pop the top two values, apply the operator, and push the result back. By the time you reach the end, exactly one value remains on the stack — the answer. This is precisely why calculators and compilers often convert expressions to postfix first: it removes the need to track precedence or parentheses at evaluation time entirely.

slides.subTitle: The shunting-yard algorithm
+, -, *, / and parentheses
When popping the operator stack
slides.markdown:
The single most common bug in infix-to-postfix conversion: popping operators off the stack using the wrong comparison, breaking either precedence or associativity.

```python
# BUG: uses > instead of >=, breaking left-associativity for equal-precedence ops
while ops and ops[-1] != '(' and PREC[ops[-1]] > PREC[tok]:
    output.append(ops.pop())
```

With `>` instead of `>=`, `"3 - 4 - 5"` (which must evaluate left-associatively as `(3-4)-5 = -6`) can get converted incorrectly, because an equal-precedence operator already on the stack never gets popped before the new one is pushed, silently changing the grouping. Left-associative operators (`+ - * /`) need `>=`; right-associative operators (like exponentiation) deliberately need strict `>`, so the correct comparison depends on the operator's associativity, not a single rule applied everywhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Recursion vs an explicit stack for expression parsing
slides.subTitle: When you need the explicit version
slides.markdown:
| | Recursive descent | Explicit stack |
|---|---|---|
| Handles nested parentheses | naturally, via recursive calls | needs manual push/pop on `(`/`)` |
| Stack usage | implicit (call stack) | explicit (a stack you manage) |
| Depth limits | bounded by language recursion limit | bounded only by available memory |
| Readability | often clearer for grammar-like expressions | more verbose but more controllable |

Recursive descent parsing handles nesting "for free" because each `(` naturally becomes a recursive call and each `)` naturally returns — the call stack **is** the stack. The explicit-stack version does the same bookkeeping manually.

The explicit version wins when input can be pathologically deeply nested (thousands of parentheses) and you can't risk hitting a language's recursion depth limit — exactly the scenario where the elegance of recursion becomes a liability rather than an asset.
